news.title: Whatley Within Striking Distance of Defeating Roy Cooper in North Carolina
news.text: Republican Michael Whatley is within striking distance of former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper in the race for North Carolina’s open U.S. Senate seat, according to a new High Point University poll released Friday. The race is for the seat currently held by Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who is not seeking reelection. Cooper, who served as North Carolina governor from 2017 through 2024, is seeking a return to elected office, while Whatley is the former chairman of the Republican National Committee (RNC) and the North Carolina Republican Party. Jeff Allen, Cooper for North Carolina campaign manager, told Newsweek via email on Friday when asked about the new poll, "Roy Cooper has spent his career putting North Carolinians first, while Washington, D.C., insider Michael Whatley spent his delivering for billionaires and special interests at the expense of the middle class. A Democrat has not won statewide federal office in North Carolina in nearly two decades and we know this race will be very close, which is why we’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them in the Senate." Newsweek also reached out to Whatley's campaign via email on Friday for comment. Why It Matters Republicans in the Senate hold a 53-45 majority—excluding independent Senators Bernie Sanders and Angus King, who caucus with Democrats—and Democrats view flipping the seat as a potential pathway to taking control of the upper chamber. Midterm elections are also commonly seen as a measure of public approval for the current president too, and the president's party has traditionally lost seats during these elections. Trump has backed Whatley in the race, adding another layer of potential intensity. What To Know The contest is viewed as one of the key Senate races of the 2026 midterms, with the outcome potentially affecting control of the chamber. The Cook Political Report has the race slated as Lean Democrat. The poll showed that among likely voters, Cooper leads Whatley 50 percent to 45 percent, a 5-point advantage that falls within the poll’s 5.2-percentage-point credibility interval. The poll shows that 3 percent are unsure or would not vote and 3 percent would pick someone else or another party. The survey of 800 self-identified registered voters, including 660 likely voters, was conducted August 3-12. The poll marks a closer contest than some recent surveys have suggested. Among all self-identified registered voters, Cooper leads Whatley 48 percent to 41 percent, with 8 percent unsure or saying they would not vote and 4 percent saying they would pick someone else or another party. The HPU poll gives that group a 4.3-percentage-point credibility interval. Grant Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek via email on Friday in part, "One has to be careful about slicing the results too thin. It was also an online poll, as I understand it. I’d be wary of investing too much meaning in a couple point shift from previous polls when the margin of error is 5 points." "But having said all that," Reeher added, "a smallish shift is not surprising, given the recent unpopularity of the Iran War, and persistent inflation and interest rate concerns. It’s still anyone’s race, even though I agree with Cook that it looks like it’s leaning toward the Dems. And Cooper may not have as much of the negativity associated with the Democratic brand as some other candidates." D. Stephen Voss, political science professor at the University of Kentucky, also told Newsweek via email on Friday: "The tightening of the North Carolina race makes sense because of the name-recognition advantage Roy Cooper enjoyed going into the contest. Likely voters knew him and many knew they were ready to support him. Fewer voters knew Michael Whatley, reporting neither a favorable nor an unfavorable opinion of him. "It makes sense that as the race gained more attention, the sort of people who typically vote Republican would be returning to the fold, leaving fewer likely voters still unsure of what they'll do. That's the educational function that election season performs. Once Whatley finishes picking up the voters who always should have been his, though, persuading the remainder will become just as hard for him as it is for Cooper," Voss concluded. The HPU poll points to a challenging political environment for Republicans in the state. Among likely voters, 59 percent say the country is on the wrong track, compared with 36 percent who say it is headed in the right direction. Trump’s approval rating stands at 42 percent, with 54 percent disapproving, while 48 percent of likely voters say North Carolina itself was on the wrong track. Those broader numbers could give Cooper an advantage, but Whatley’s five-point deficit among likely voters is close enough that the race remains competitive with less than three months until Election Day. Trump won the swing state in the 2024 presidential election versus former Vice President Kamala Harris by 3.3 percent. What Other Polls Show Other recent polling has generally shown Cooper with a larger advantage. An Elon University poll released earlier this month found Cooper ahead of Whatley 53 percent to 42 percent among likely voters. The poll surveyed 800 North Carolina adults from July 23 to July 31, 2026, and has a margin of error of 5.6 percent for likely voters. A Carolina Journal Poll shows Cooper leading with 51.5 percent to Whatley's 39 percent. The survey, conducted by Harper Polling, was from August 9 to August 10, 2026, and has a margin of error of 4 percent. What's Next for Whatley and Cooper Neither campaign has published a public calendar of events for the upcoming week; however, here's what's expected: Both campaigns appear to be ramping up in-person events as the November 3 election approaches and recent polling continues to show a competitive race. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas

news.title: California’s Home of Chicken and Waffles suddenly shuts down after 20-year run
news.text:
Get clucked, the kitchen is closing.

After a decades-long run dishing up chicken and waffles, an Oakland staple is closing its doors for good. Home of Chicken and Waffles announced the closure on its website telling guests its last day to scarf down a plate will be on August 31.

“Thank you for all the years of love and friendship!” The spot wrote.

The closing brings the end of a 23-year long era, as founder Derreck Johnson first opened the joint back in 2004 at its first location on Embarcadero West. It later moved to its current spot on Fourth Street in 2024.

The southern staple was not only known for its soul food but its community outreach as it employed formerly incarcerated workers. The spot also drew high-profile customers like Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris.

Johnson told SF Gate he is “Very happy and excited about [closing].” After 23 years, I want out of the restaurant business. I’m just ready to move on.” 

The restaurant did not give a specific reason behind the closure but Johnson told multiple outlets that he is looking forward to the next chapter and will announce more details about the future in the coming months.

Customers flooded to social media after the announcement with lifelong eaters mourning. 

“Awwww Derrick’s presence and food has been a legendary comfort to so many folks here! Wishing my frat brother much success and love for what comes next!” One wrote on Instagram.

On remembering what Johnson did for the community, one customer commented, “job well done, you’ve helped sooooooo many of us & helped us become who we are today thank you so much for the opportunity & the love you. Poured into us all we were family & many of us are still connected looking forward to what’s to come ahead.”

Another Bay Area favorite is closed down after nearly 15 years. Pucquio, a Peruvian restaurant in Rockridge, served up its last dish back in July.

The spot announced the shutter on Instagram, stunning customers. 

“A chapter is closing, but the memories we’ve shared will last forever. Thank you for every visit, every celebration, and for allowing us to share the flavors of Peru with you. It has been an honor to be part of your story,” the Oakland spot said.

news.title: Trump underwater in 47 states and DC, new projection finds
news.text:
Amid President Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings nationally, a new YouGov/Economist projection shows the president's net job approval is negative in all but three states.

According to The Economist and YouGov, more people disapprove than approve of Trump’s job performance in 47 out of 50 states and in the District of Columbia. The three states where the majority of respondents still approve of the president are Wyoming (+14), Idaho (+9), and West Virginia (+6). 

All three went for Trump in the 2016, 2020, and 2020 presidential elections.

The lowest net job approval rating for Trump was in D.C. (-83). The two states that disapprove of the president's job the most are Maryland and Vermont, both at -50. The three are all historically Democratic strongholds that voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

The White House did not immediately respond to USA TODAY’s request for comment on Friday, Aug. 21.

See map of Trump’s net approval

A historic run

Trump’s negative net approval in most states in the country comes as the president continues to see record-low approval numbers in nationwide polling.

In a new Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Aug. 17, only one in three Americans said they approved of Trump’s job performance, the lowest approval rating the president has seen in Reuters/Ipsos tracking since his return to the White House in 2025.

Trump’s bad polling numbers come as an overwhelming majority of Americans said they were concerned that the war against Iran would continue for an extended period.

In the Aug. 17 poll, 80% of Americans, including 87% of Democrats and 71% of Republicans, believed the U.S. involvement with Iran would continue for an “extended period of time.”

What do polling averages show?

While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to show Trump in negative territory overall:

RealClearPolitics (Aug. 21): 39.5% approve, 57.2% disapproveNew York Times (Aug. 21): 37% approve, 59% disapproveSilver Bulletin (Aug. 21): 38.2% approve, 57.9% disapprove

USA TODAY’s Kinsey Crowley contributed to this report.

news.title: A Massachusetts primary tests Democrats’ appetite to ‘change the culture’
news.text:
PEABODY, Mass. — The 2026 midterm primary cycle has been a year of tests — both ideological and generational — for Democrats across the nation. 

A race for a House seat north of Boston poses another question: Are voters looking for a candidate with powerful connections and a raft of experience or are they seeking a Washington outsider who promises to take on the party establishment?

At a recent forum here for the Democrats vying for Massachusetts’ 6th District, anti-incumbent fervor was on full display.

“We keep electing D.C. insiders … playing by the old playbook,” said state Rep. Tram Nguyen. 

“People are fed up with the status quo,’’ asserted another candidate, fintech executive John Beccia.

“The Democratic Party is broken, figuratively and financially,’’ offered a third, former state Rep. Jamie Belsito.

But there’s a twist to this contest: Unlike other recent primaries in blue districts, where entrenched Democrats have lost to Washington outsiders, there’s no incumbent on the Sept. 1 ballot. The seat is open because six-term Rep. Seth Moulton opted for a Senate run.

Enter Dan Koh, whom most of the field is treating as the de facto incumbent — even though the only elective office he’s held was a single term on the Andover Select Board. He also ran for the nearby 3rd District in 2018, narrowly losing the Democratic nomination to Lori Trahan.

But Koh has deep ties to the Democratic Party establishment, having served as a senior adviser to former President Joe Biden and as an aide to former Labor Secretary and Boston Mayor Martin J. Walsh. 

On the campaign trail, he says his experience in Washington makes him a battle-tested advocate who will aggressively push back against the Trump administration. 

“People want fighters against this president who are going to hold him accountable,’’ he said in an interview before the Peabody forum. “I've been out there using the experience I had in the Biden White House, working in the Cabinet.”

Massachusetts state Rep. Tram Nguyen and former congressional aide Mariah Lancaster attend the Aug. 15 event in Peabody, Mass., for Democratic candidates running for the state's 6th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A Democratic divide

Massachusetts’ 6th District hugs the Atlantic coast in the state’s northeastern corner and includes old-money towns, busy suburbs and working-class enclaves. Four days before the Peabody forum, The Boston Globe declared that the historic North Shore city, once a hub of leather manufacturing, was home to the nation’s hottest housing market.

Six Democrats are competing for the nomination to succeed Moulton in what is the Bay State’s only open seat. Koh, Beccia and Nguyen have been the leading fundraisers. Other hopefuls include software engineer Bethany Andres-Beck and former State Department and congressional aide Mariah Lancaster. 

Kamala Harris carried the seat by 21 points in 2024, according to calculation by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, so whoever wins the primary is likely to prevail in November over Republican Army veteran Micah Jones. 

Koh has the backing of two pillars of Democratic politics: Biden and Harris, both of whom appear on his behalf in a new ad.

But Biden’s protracted departure from the 2024 presidential race following his flailing debate performance — and Harris’ subsequent loss to Trump — has frustrated many grassroots Democrats. The starring role that the two onetime standard-bearers are playing in Koh’s campaign risks serving as an uncomfortable reminder of a painful episode for the party.

[Roll Call on the Road: New England]

Koh said Biden’s endorsement — one of just a few that the former president has made this cycle — still carries weight with Democratic primary voters. 

“Plenty of people have their differences with the president,’’ he said. “But they remember what it was like when there was a president that they actually could look up to and admire, one that honored the presidency.” 

Others aren’t so sure. “I would not personally put Biden’s endorsement on my webpage,” said Andres-Beck.

Koh’s supporters, though, say his Washington connections are assets that would help him deliver for the district.

“We need a congressman who knows the lay of the land and can get things done,’’ said John F. Tierney, a Democrat who held the seat for nearly two decades before losing to Moulton in a 2014 primary. “Dan is very capable of getting around in Washington and working with everybody there.”

Former Massachusetts state Rep. Jamie Belsito greets attendees at the Aug. 15 candidate forum in Peabody, Mass., for Democratic contenders for the 6th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

For some voters, knowing your way around Washington is a liability, not an advantage. 

“In the Democratic Party, we consistently mistake a fancy resume for real experience,’’ said Tristan R. Brown, a data privacy attorney from Peabody who attended the forum. “These things are not the same, and if we want to be a party of working-class people, we need working-class candidates who can actually speak from experience.”

Brown, 41, said he’s backing Belsito because of her blue-collar roots and progressive policies: “We’ve got to change the culture.’’ 

Nguyen has also emphasized her hardscrabble upbringing as a refugee from Vietnam who grew up in public housing and “knows what it’s like to stand in a food pantry line.”

“People are feeling as though elected officials are detached from their lives,’’ she said at the Peabody forum. “That’s why we need new voices and fresh perspectives and people with lived experience going to Congress.”

The race heats up

In the final sprint before the primary, the race has grown increasingly heated. Koh, who brought in $4.5 million through June 30, has faced attacks from Beccia, who is largely self-funding his race. 

Businessman John Beccia speaks at the Aug. 15 Democratic candidate forum in Peabody, Mass., for 6th District contenders. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outside groups are also spending: Super PACs backing Nguyen and Koh have flooded mailboxes with attack ads.

At the candidates forum, held in a Veterans of Foreign Wars hall decorated with red, white and blue balloons, attacks on Trump were interspersed with lacing criticism of the Democratic Party. 

“I know that my faith in the Democratic Party is shaken, and I suspect in this room I am not alone in that,” said Lancaster, “because we know that even as Democrats, we have not been delivering for working families.”

Democrats, Belsito said, “are not taking care of people, we are only taking care of special interests and people are done.”

Still, some voters believe the differences among the field, while significant, are a sign of the party’s strength. 

“We have six excellent candidates,’’ said Mary Duff Henry, a union activist from Peabody who had yet to make up her mind.. “We’ll have excellent representation no matter who wins.”

Engineer Beth Andres-Beck, a Democratic candidate for Massachusetts’ 6th District, attends the Aug. 15 event in Peabody, Mass. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

news.title: Kylie Kelce reveals Taylor Swift's surprising family nickname
news.text:
Taylor Swift is officially part of the Kelce family, and she's got the title to prove it.

Kylie Kelce, whose brother-in-law Travis Kelce married the pop star earlier this summer, revealed Swift's new family nickname during a recent episode of her podcast, "Not Gonna Lie," released Thursday, Aug. 20.

Swift and the NFL star tied the knot at Madison Square Garden on July 3. The star-studded nuptials featured a bevy of A-list guests, including Ed Sheeran, Gigi Hadid and Bradley Cooper, Tom Cruise, Adam Sandler and Zoë Kravitz.

Kylie Kelce's husband, Travis' brother Jason Kelce, served as best man, while their four daughters − Wyatt, Elliotte, Bennett and Finnley − were flower girls.

Speaking with actress Leslie Mann during the episode, Kylie Kelce brought up Swift and her growing influence on the Kelce clan.

The podcaster pointed out that Mann is a "cat person," which she said was an opportunity to brainstorm how to "convince my husband to let me get a cat."

"I grew up with cats. So, I grew up in a cat-dog house, like, both at all times. And now our kids have influences in their life," the 34-year-old said. "Aunt Taylor is a big one, where they get to be around cats. And then we go home, and there are no cats."

Kylie Kelce previously dished on how her daughters reacted when the newlyweds got engaged. “The girls are thrilled," she told Good Morning America back in September 2025. "They’re so excited they’re getting another aunt. And we could not be more excited for them and what the future holds. We love love, and we love Taylor and Trav."

Kylie Kelce speaks out: Podcaster on being 'terrified' about pregnancy after miscarriage

It's no secret Aunt Taylor, 36, has become quite the cat lover over the years.

The "Fate of Ophelia" singer's three cats − Meredith Grey, Olivia Benson and Benjamin Button − have each achieved celebrity status in their own right, thanks to their frequent cat cameos on Swift's social media.

During the 2024 presidential election, the pop superstar posed with Benjamin Button for a politically charged post endorsing former Vice President Kamala Harris. Swift referred to herself as a "childless cat lady" in its caption, a direct dig at comments made by President Donald Trump's running mate and current VP, JD Vance.

Kylie Kelce said that although her husband, Jason, has reservations about getting a cat – including his allergy to the animal – she hopes to get the pet by next summer.

"It's gotten to the point where every time we go somewhere that [the kids] get to pick out a reward, if there's anything cat related, they're getting it," she said. "And I'm like, 'Jason, I need you to lock in here. There is cat need in this house.'"

Kylie Kelce opens up about emotional Taylor Swift, Travis Kelce wedding

On the Aug. 6 episode of "Not Gonna Lie," Kylie Kelce revealed that her husband, Jason, became very emotional during Swift and Travis Kelce's wedding at Madison Square Garden.

After discussing Jason crying at his own nuptials to Kylie in 2018, the podcaster said, "More importantly, he cried at his brother's wedding for many reasons."

"It was touching, it was very loving to see all the things that were happening," Kelce added.

Kylie Kelce talks Taylor Swift wedding: 'Not Gonna Lie' host reveals who cried at MSG wedding

Kelce has been tight-lipped about sharing further details of the celebrity wedding, but she did shed some light on what made Jason choke up.

"Take this into consideration 'cause no one's thinking about this: think about getting to watch your four daughters be flower girls," she said. "OK, that's all the information you get. It was emotional, and he was not the only adult crying in our family."

Contributing: Melina Khan, Anika Reed and Bryan West, USA TODAY

news.title: Kamala Harris reaches for Nazi slogan on Stacey Abrams' podcast
news.text:
Earlier this month, Kamala Harris made an appearance on Stacey Abrams' podcast “Assembly Required,” where they discussed the Democratic Party’s future, redistricting in the South, voter ID debates, and opposing what they framed as Trump’s authoritarian agenda.

In their conversation about citizenship and who counts as a “legitimate” American, Harris deployed a predictable Nazi analogy.

“Part of the pain of this moment, Stacey, is these so-called leaders who are pushing this kind of narrative about who is a legitimate American citizen among American citizens. This blood-and-soil narrative that’s being pushed at the highest levels of our government to suggest that, you know, once again to hearken back to times when it was explicit that there was a hierarchy among Americans and who was superior and who was inferior — all citizens,” the failed 2024 nominee said.

“That’s what’s happening right now,” she added.

“I follow politics quite a bit, and I've not heard anyone talking about blood-and-soil Americans,” says BlazeTV host Pat Gray.

“I have heard the guy that used to be her boss talk about the blood of liberty,” adds co-host Jeffy, referring to Joe Biden’s dismissal of Thomas Jefferson’s line about the tree of liberty being watered with the blood of patriots as “a bunch of crap.”

Pat believes Harris must “babble about something” because “she’s getting no love from Democrats right now.”

“I don't know why, with such, you know, insightful thoughts like that,” laughs Jeffy.

news.title: Florida Politics Embody How Black People Are Not a Monolith — For Better And Worse [Op-Ed]
news.text:
If you ever needed proof that the adage, “all skinfolk ain’t kinfolk,” is true, the race to the 2026 midterms in Florida stands as evidence.

Byron Donalds is attempting to do what Andrew Gillum couldn’t do back in 2018: become Florida’s first Black governor, but as a Republican. To put it nicely, Donalds makes Clarence Thomas look like Marcus Garvey. This is a man who thought the case against Trump for his mishandling of classified documents was “insane” because it “never made sense” to him why people were upset that his “friend” had boxes of top-secret documents stored in his shower. This is also a man who supports ICE and legitimately thought he had a shot at being Trump’s pick for vice president.

Donalds is the living and breathing version of Stephen from the 2012 film “Django Unchained.” Yet, surprisingly, he’s the favorite to become Florida’s next leader.

“I stand before a sea of conservative patriots who seek to take the reins of power from the progressive left,” he declared all the way back in 2010. Since then, he’s done and said whatever was necessary to work himself to this point, because as we know — if you want to skip the line in politics as a Black person in America, run as a Republican. “The payoff was huge. A month after President Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he backed Mr. Donalds to be the next governor of Florida, the president’s adopted home state, before he had even declared his candidacy,” read a report from the New York Times on Donalds’ ascendance in the GOP. “On Tuesday, Mr. Donalds, 47, easily captured the Republican nomination to lead the nation’s third largest state, making him the front-runner in the November general election against David Jolly, the Democratic nominee,” the report noted.

For a culture and community often forced to support each other despite individual missteps and flawed views, some see Donalds as caught between a rock and a hard place. Depending on one’s perspective, he might be seen as someone Harriet Tubman would have left behind or as “a brotha who is just doing what he has to do.”

Neither position is one that’s enviable or desired.

However, given the fight that we take part in to be seen as more than, Donalds is weirdly a necessity, as he serves as a paragon of our diversity.

On the other hand, Angie Nixon is on the doorstep of doing the impossible — winning a statewide election without a war chest and national name recognition as a Black female progressive Democrat in the South. The state representative from Duval County recently won the Senate nomination. Nixon is an underdog and a union organizer who ran a grassroots campaign and is up against a white female Republican incumbent as a double minority in a state with an unpleasant past.

“They look at this movement, and they call us extreme, they call us radical, but I think people see through that,” Nixon declared after her victory, as her campaign slogan reads, ‘Change Can’t Wait.’

“I won’t let them define me, and I know you will always know where I stand,” she added. “If believing a mom shouldn’t have to work three jobs to keep a roof over her head is extreme, call me extreme. Ashley Moody (the incumbent) can call me whatever she wants, but in November she’ll be calling me senator.”

For all the hemming and hawing many Democrats have done during the Trump era, frustrated that their party doesn’t have a candidate willing to give Republicans a taste of their own medicine, Nixon checks those boxes in many ways. However, in a post-Kamala Harris world, while it’s refreshing to see a darker-skinned Black woman get to this point, it’s beyond reasonable to wonder if “they” will be willing to cast their ballots for her in November.

Because, as we know. Just because a Black woman is the best person for the job doesn’t mean she’s even guaranteed an interview.

“Is Florida ready for a democratic socialist candidate in a general election? I still don’t know the answer,” Aubrey Jewett, professor of political science at the University of Central Florida, recently told The Guardian about Nixon. “But what this primary showed was that, within the Democratic Party base, there is a strong majority of progressive social Democrats in Florida – just like there apparently is across the country.”

What Donalds and Nixon represent in Florida is taking place at a pivotal moment. It is impossible to talk about Black achievement in that state without mentioning and thinking of Gillum — and his past and current legal troubles — particularly when it comes to what Donalds is trying to accomplish. Florida is also home to one of the largest HBCUs, Florida A&M University, which was embroiled in controversy last year when Gov. Ron DeSantis’ ally Marva Johnson was appointed president despite boisterous opposition from the student body and alumni base, thus leading to her being deemed “MAGA Marva.”

The ideology surrounding which people and institutions deserve our grace and protection has always been an ongoing, contextual conversation within our community. We are even watching it play out in the media landscape with the debate about whether or not the National Association of Black Journalists was justified in giving ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith a “thumbs down” for his repeated negative commentary towards his own people, particularly Black women.

In a country where our image matters more and our representation has to be fought for, our willingness to “look out for each other” has become a necessity driven by survival instincts. However, just because the crusade for appreciation of the spectrum of our humanity continues, it doesn’t mean we have to support those who stand against us just because they look like us. Nothing represents that sentiment more than the opposing options Black voters in Florida will have on Election Day.

Carron J. Phillips is an award-winning journalist who writes on race, culture, social issues, politics, and sports. He hails from Saginaw, Michigan, and is a graduate of Morehouse College and Syracuse University. Follow his Substack to keep up with more of his work.

news.title: No, Ro, You Won't Outflank AOC to Snag the Democratic Nomination for President
news.text:
I've said a lot of stupid things over the years, and I do my best to acknowledge them when I discover that I am wrong. 

And if there is one category of things about which I am most often wrong, it's granting people more grace than they deserve because I was not cynical enough about their motives. 

Don't get me wrong: I am very cynical about institutions, but I still have a weakness that often causes me trouble, although I am loath to correct it nonetheless, and that is the Pollyanna-ish hope that the individual people I observe really might not be money- or power-hungry to the extent that they will throw ethics to the side in order to get ahead. 

I KNOW that there are good people out there, so I try to assume the best in people until they prove themselves unworthy. 

Man, am I often wrong on that!

Ro Khanna is a case in point. Back when he was just a liberal congressman and not a candidate for president, unannounced as he is, Khanna struck me as basically honest and decent, and merely too liberal for my tastes and more than a bit wrong on economics. 

It turns out that Khanna wasn't thoughtful or decent, though; he was just cosplaying being a decent liberal in order to con his Silicon Valley constituents into supporting him. He seemed to be a business-friendly liberal who understood startup culture but didn't understand that while tech companies can afford outrageous pay and benefits, small businesses can't, and high taxes would kill them. 

Now that he has basically thrown his hat into the ring in the race for the Democrat Party nomination for president, he has turned into something unrecognizable: a Hasan Piker advocate who wants to destroy capitalism, all while hiding his own wealth and promoting ideas he most certainly knows will destroy the country.

news.title: Republicans’ Chances of Flipping New Hampshire Senate Seat—Poll
news.text: Republicans view the New Hampshire U.S. Senate race as one of their few pickup opportunities in this year's midterm elections, but a poll released this week showed Democratic Representative Chris Pappas with a lead over his two potential Republican rivals. Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen is retiring at the end of her term, opening a seat in a state that former Vice President Kamala Harris won by 3 points in the 2024 presidential election. New Hampshire is often decided by slim margins, though it has backed Democrats in federal races over the past decade. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in the midterms, and President Donald Trump’s approval rating has slipped over the past few months amid growing economic concerns around the cost of living and inflation, so Democrats believe they will have an advantage in the state. But Republicans believe its open-seat status and a strong candidate could put the race in play for them. Pappas is viewed as the front-runner to win the Democratic nomination against progressive Karishma Manzur, while former New Hampshire Senator John Sununu has led September 8 primary polls against former Massachusetts Senator Scott Brown for the GOP. Newsweek reached out to the Brown, Manzur, Pappas and Sununu campaigns for comment via email. Chris Pappas Leads New Hampshire Senate Poll The St. Anselm College poll released on Thursday found that Pappas would have an advantage over Brown and Sununu in the general election. Sununu, who held the Senate seat from 2003 to 2009, held Pappas to a closer race than Brown, who represented Massachusetts in the Senate from 2010 to 2013, according to the poll. Pappas held a 7-point lead over Sununu, 48 percent to 41 percent, and a 12-point lead over Brown, 49 percent to 37 percent, the poll found. Pappas also held a large lead over Manzur in the Democratic primary, 59 percent to 28 percent. On the Republican side, Sununu led Brown by 30 points, 54 percent to 24 percent. The poll was conducted August 17-18 among 1,411 likely voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points. Pappas has represented New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District—viewed as the more competitive of the state's two districts—since 2019. Prior to entering Congress, he served as a member of the New Hampshire Executive Council. His family owns the Manchester restaurant Puritan Backroom that has been credited with inventing chicken tenders. What Other Polls Show Other polling has shown Pappas with a lead, though surveys suggest a very close race. A Peak Insights poll, sponsored by the National Republican Senatorial Committee, found Pappas up only a single point, 43 percent to 42 percent. It polled 500 likely voters June 24-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. A University of New Hampshire poll, conducted among 2,232 likely voters June 18-23, showed Pappas up 3 points against Sununu, 47 percent to 44 percent, and 14 points against Brown, 52 percent to 38 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.1 percentage points. Meanwhile, a poll from Emerson College earlier this year showed Pappas up 1 point against Sununu, 45 percent to 44 percent, and 9 points over Brown, 48 percent to 39 percent. It surveyed 1,100 likely voters March 21-23 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball view the race as Lean Democratic. Democrats Favored in Prediction Markets Prediction markets show Democrats as favorites to hold onto the seat in November. Kalshi gave Democrats an 89 percent chance of winning the race, while Democrats’ chances stood at 86 percent on Polymarket as of Friday afternoon. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Republican Kelly Ayotte Favored in Governor's Race The new St. Anselm College poll showed that Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte has a lead over Democrat Cinde Warmington in the gubernatorial race. Although the state leans Democrat on the federal level, Republicans have been on a winning streak in gubernatorial races, winning every race since 2016. The poll gave Ayotte an 11-point lead, 49 percent to 38 percent, with 13 percent remaining undecided. Independents Key to New Hampshire Winning over independents is critical to victory in New Hampshire as undeclared voters make up the largest portion of the electorate. In total, 351,815 New Hampshirites were not registered with either party, according to the New Hampshire secretary of state’s office as of August 3. There were 299,976 registered Republicans and 247,069 registered Democrats. In 2024, the state narrowly went to Harris, 50.7 percent to 47.9 percent. But it gave former President Joe Biden a wider victory in 2020, backing him by a 7-point margin. In 2016, it was one of the closest races in the country, backing former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton by less than half a percentage point. New Hampshire’s southern and central region is fairly dense around cities like Manchester, Concord, Portsmouth, Dover and Nashua. Many of those cities are more Democratic, though not always overwhelmingly. Manchester, for instance backed Harris by less than 8 points in 2024. But many of the suburbs and smaller towns in southern New Hampshire are more Republican. College towns like Durham and Keene are also critical for Democrats in the state. The northern part is more rural. Areas in the White Mountains have a Democratic lean due to its dependence on tourism, though some other more sparsely populated areas are more conservative. New Hampshire is generally viewed as politically moderate with a libertarian streak, and it has been willing to back politicians from both parties over the years. Can Democrats Win Senate Control? New Hampshire is a must-win for Democrats if they want to flip control of the Senate. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, so Democrats must defend all of their seats and flip four others to take control of the upper chamber of Congress. Democrats are facing a difficult map, defending seats in two states Trump won in 2024—Georgia and Michigan. In Michigan, polls show a tight race between progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, while Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff has built a polling lead over Representative Mike Collins in Georgia. Maine and North Carolina are viewed as Democrats’ top flip opportunities. In Maine, which Harris won by about 7 points, longtime GOP Senator Susan Collins is up for reelection. She faces Democrat Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president, won the nomination in a special election after scandal-plagued Graham Platner exited the race following a primary victory. Collins has shown a remarkable ability to win elections in Maine as she seeks her sixth term. In North Carolina, which Trump won by about 3 points, Democratic former Governor Roy Cooper has built a polling lead against Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee. Republican Senator Thom Tillis is retiring. But even if Democrats win all of those races, Republicans will still have a 51-49 majority, so Democrats must win at least two seats in states Trump won by double digits in 2024 to take control. Democrats view Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas as being potentially competitive, and polls show close races in those states. If Republicans pull off a victory in New Hampshire, Democrats will then need to flip three of those seats, a more difficult feat given their conservative leans. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Republicans view New Hampshire as a potential pickup opportunity in the upper chamber of Congress in the midterms.

news.title: Trump’s TikTok Strategy Has Become Punk Rock for the Right
news.text: When Ariana Grande told the Trump administration in June to stop using her music after the White House posted a video of ICE arrests to her track "Bye," the administration responded in true Trump style: it used another one of her songs in yet another politically charged video. This time, the track in question was Grande's "We Can’t Be Friends (Wait for Your Love)," attached to a TikTok about transgender athletes. Grande appeared in the comments with an unambiguous comment: "Never use my music again. Again. Grande isn’t alone in her response to what some might call musical flattery. Taylor Swift, Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo and Katy Perry have all objected to Trump or his administration using their music. Beyoncé’s representatives also intervened when Trump’s 2024 campaign used "Freedom," which happened to be the same song Kamala Harris had made part of her own campaign soundtrack, without pushback from the artist. So Trump is dealing with a string of unwanted celebrity endorsements…or is he? Upon closer inspection, some might argue that this is less of a problem for Trump than a voluntary format. The president has taken one of the oldest complaints in conservative politics—that Hollywood and popular culture belong to the left—and arrived at a characteristically Trumpian solution: use their supposedly left-leaning stuff anyway. Better still, from the perspective of the attention economy, the artist may then complain, giving Trump’s decision to use the material a second life. The cycle is easy to follow: fans pile in, the media writes about it, and Trump never quite leaves the news cycle. And there is evidence that, at least sometimes, this is exactly the point. After a previous controversy over the White House using Swift’s music, an administration official told Variety that the post was made knowing news organizations would amplify the dispute: "Congrats, you got played." To keep the musical theme going, it almost seems as if Trump’s social-media politics has become a kind of punk rock for the right. The fact that the song is forbidden makes it more useful and the artist’s disapproval completes the performance. When the Backlash Becomes the Content By now, the Trump playbook is filled with examples, starting with Swift, which offers perhaps the clearest one. Earlier this month, Team Trump posted a TikTok using Swift’s "August" over footage of the president and first lady Melania Trump watching fireworks alongside the caption: "I’m sure @TaylorSwift is going to be super excited we used her song!" Swift’s fans immediately took to social media to complain, but their comments fueled stories in the media, making their reaction just as central to the discussion as Trump’s choice of music. The audio was eventually removed, a development that was also reported on for days. Carpenter’s example goes a bit further. After the White House put "Juno" over footage of immigration arrests in December, she called the video "evil and disgusting" and told the administration not to involve her music in its "inhumane agenda." The White House then answered her publicly with a statement packed with references to her own songs, turning her objection into another round of content. The pattern repeated with Rodrigo, who objected after the White House and Department of Homeland Security used "All-American B****" in a video promoting self-deportation, and Katy Perry, who protested after "Firework" was paired with footage of U.S. military strikes. In each case, the artist’s rejection became part of the story surrounding the original post, extending its life beyond the White House’s own audience. The precedent goes back further, though. During the 2024 campaign, Trump spokesman Steven Cheung posted a video of Trump arriving in Michigan set to Beyoncé’s "Freedom"—the same song the singer had authorized Kamala Harris to use. Beyoncé’s representatives objected, but the dispute only sharpened the provocation: Trump had briefly appropriated the opposition’s soundtrack. When the Song Changes Sides Then there is "Y.M.C.A.," which complicates the story. Village People frontman Victor Willis first asked Trump to stop using the group’s music in June 2020, after Trump threatened to deploy the military during protests following George Floyd’s killing. The group’s manager later sent a cease-and-desist in 2023 over a Mar-a-Lago performance that used Village People’s image and music. But Trump kept playing "Y.M.C.A." and, crucially, kept dancing to it. The stiff fist-pumping routine became a meme in its own right in 2020 and returned after the 2024 election. By late 2024, Willis had changed his position, now arguing that Trump appeared to genuinely enjoy the song and had helped push it back up the charts. The band even performed the track at Trump's 2025 pre-inauguration rally, where he joined them on stage for the now famous dance. It is an unusually neat example of where repeated cultural appropriation can end up: the meme became bigger than the objection, and the song acquired a second political life of its own. Is Swift about to headline Mar-a-Lago? Although we haven't asked her, we can confidently say that's not likely to happen—but Trump doesn't really need her to perform at one of his events to coast on the artist's immense fame. Sometimes, the win is simply making someone else’s song feel like part of the Trump show anyway.
news.summary: Trump’s use of pop music is turning celebrity backlash into another tool for attention, outrage and political branding.
news.author: Anna Rahmanan

news.title: Vivek Ramaswamy slammed for $700K private jet scheme: 'Using donor funds to pay himself'
news.text:
Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy spent hundreds of thousands of dollars of campaign funds leasing a private jet from a company he owns, records show.

Of nearly $690,000 that his campaign spent on private jets, nearly $560,000 of that went to V Leasing LLC — a company whose listed address is a house Ramaswamy owns — according to the Ohio Capital Journal. Ramaswamy has loaned his campaign more than $25 million, the report said. 

In May, Ramaswamy told a Youngstown news station he preferred to drive, the Journal noted.

"I love long drives," he said. "You think about the time we spend in Trumbull County, and you think about the time we even spend just going for a nice jog. You think about Cuyahoga National Park, not far from where we are. I'm a nature guy."

Campaign finance records reviewed by the Ohio Capital Journal show his campaign also paid nearly $130,000 to TVPX Aircraft Solutions in Salt Lake City.

Ramaswamy's campaign did not respond to questions the Ohio Capital Journal sent multiple times, the outlet reported.

Jordan Libowitz, vice president in communications for the nonprofit watchdog Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, told the Journal that the loan structure creates a path for self-payment.

"If he is basically fronting money to rent a plane from himself, and then if he does not forgive the loans but reimburses himself, he'll essentially be using donor funds to pay himself," Libowitz told the outlet.

Federal flight records show Ramaswamy flew between Columbus and Cleveland and between Columbus and Akron on his private jet, the Ohio Capital Journal reported.

"The fact that Ramaswamy has spent two years flying around on his own private jet is really a bad look," David Cohen, political science professor and director of the Applied Politics Program at the University of Akron's Bliss Institute, explained to the outlet.

"I mean, let's face it: Ohio is not California or Texas. You can drive from border to border in Ohio in a few hours," Cohen added. "He's flying between Columbus and Akron for crying out loud, and Columbus and Cleveland. That's a two hour drive. Get in the car."

Democratic political strategist Mike Nellis, who previously worked for Kamala Harris, wrote on X that Ramaswamy had been boasting about driving while quietly using his private jet.

"He's been bragging on the campaign trail about driving around Ohio, and it turns out he's completely full of s—," Nellis wrote. "What an awful candidate."

"It would even be funny if the nonstop lying weren't also totally disqualifying," Democratic Governors Association deputy communications director Izzi Levy wrote on X.

news.title: Republicans Dealt Quadruple Polling Blow in Race Against Abdul El-Sayed
news.text: Republicans were dealt a quadruple polling blow in the Michigan Senate race this week as four new polls gave progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed a lead over former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican. El-Sayed’s victory over centrist Representative Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary created anxiety among some in the party about their chances in Michigan, a critical swing state—particularly after a recent Fox News poll showed Rogers with a lead. Some Democrats fear El-Sayed may be too far left for such an evenly divided state. The Michigan Senate race is one of the most important Senate races of the 2026 midterms, as Democrats’ chances of flipping control of the Senate run through the Great Lakes State. A Democratic loss in Michigan, a seat currently held by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, would significantly complicate their path to a majority. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats during the midterms, so Democrats have been hopeful about their chances of winning in swing states. But Republicans do see an opportunity in the state, hoping that Rogers can win over moderate voters who may not be aligned with El-Sayed’s more progressive brand of politics. Abdul El-Sayed Leads Four New Polls of Michigan Senate Race The series of polls showed El-Sayed with narrow, single-digit leads, meaning the race against Rogers is still expected to be competitive in November. However, they may be welcome news for Democrats after some polling around the primary gave Rogers an advantage. An AARP poll released on Thursday found El-Sayed leading Rogers by a single point, 48 percent to 47 percent. El-Sayed received support from 91 percent of Democratic respondents, while Rogers received support from 96 percent of Republicans. Independents narrowly broke for El-Sayed, 48 percent to 42 percent. There are signs in the poll El-Sayed still has work to do in consolidating the base. He had a 41-point lead among Black voters. Although that’s a lead, it is much more narrow than former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 76-point win among Black voters in Michigan during the 2024 election, per CNN exit poll data. It surveyed 877 likely voters from August 9 to 11, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points. It was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research. Meanwhile, a survey from Susquehanna Polling & Research, Inc. showed El-Sayed up 7 points, 46 percent to 39 percent. “Despite public media reports that El-Sayed is facing a divided Democratic electorate after a bruising and closely contested August 4th primary, he leads Rogers 91 percent to 0 percent with self-identified Democrats and leads Rogers 46 percent to 24 percent, with Independents and unaffiliated voters,” the polling report reads. Both candidates had negative favorability, according to the poll. Forty-five percent of respondents said they viewed El-Sayed unfavorably, while 31 percent viewed him favorably. Meanwhile, 37 percent viewed Rogers unfavorably, while 28 percent viewed him positively. A key problem for Rogers in the poll is that most Michigan voters disapprove of President Donald Trump’s job performance. Democrats hope to make the midterms a referendum on Trump, and his approval has sunk nationwide as inflation and the cost of living remain high, particularly as the Iran War has sent gas prices surging. In the poll, 56 percent said they disapproved of Trump and 38 percent approved of him. It surveyed 800 likely voters from August 11 to 17, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.46 percentage points. A TIPP Insights poll, sponsored by the Republican group League of American Workers, showed El-Sayed up 3 points, 45 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 1,215 likely voters from August 6 to 10, with a credibility interval of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points among the likely voter sample. Furthermore, a GBAO poll, sponsored by the Senate Majority PAC, showed El-Sayed up 6 points, 50 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 800 likely voters from August 6 to 10 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the El-Sayed and Rogers campaigns for comment via email. Fox News Poll Stirred Democrats’ Anxiety Earlier in August, a poll from Fox News, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, showed Rogers with a 4-point lead, 51 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 1,006 registered voters from August 6 to 10 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Before the primary, an EPIC-MRA/MIRS poll showed Rogers up 3 points over El-Sayed, 46 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 600 voters from July 24 to 31, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Some Democrats viewed those polls as underscoring electability concerns around El-Sayed. Ellis Bates of VoteHub wrote in a post to X about the Fox News poll, “Michigan is the only battleground Senate race Fox News has polled where Republicans are ahead. Democrats lead in Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Texas, and Maine. That makes this a particularly rough poll for the El-Sayed campaign.” Democratic strategist Mike Hellis wrote, “A pretty sobering poll for Abdul, but lot of time left to turn it around.” El-Sayed’s performance in the primary also drew attention. Although he led polls against Stevens by a larger margin, he ended up winning by only a single point. It’s unclear whether the polling error would be replicated in the general election. A Divisive Primary El-Sayed emerged victorious from a contentious primary against Stevens, a centrist representing the suburbs of Detroit in Congress. U.S. support for Israel became a major sticking point in the primary and could continue to be a factor in November, as Michigan is home to notable Arab American and Jewish populations. Many Democrats believe former Vice President Kamala Harris lost votes in the state because of her support for Israel. El-Sayed has cast himself as a critic of the Israeli government. Some Michigan Democrats have declined to say they would support El-Sayed as the nominee. Representative Hillary Scholten, who represents a district based around Grand Rapids, told Semafor that she would “not stand beside someone who has allowed distinctly anti-American sentiment to enter our public dialogue.” This week, Michigan state Representative Karen Whitsett attended an event as part of a “Democrats for Rogers” coalition. According to Michigan Advance, she said during the event that health care is a key issue for her driving her support for Rogers, as El-Sayed has been a supporter of Medicare for All. “You will lose your health insurance if the other candidate gets in office. There’s no ifs, ands, or buts about it. That is what Medicare for all means,” she said, according to the report. What Prediction Markets Show Prediction markets gave El-Sayed an advantage over Rogers on Friday. On Kalshi, El-Sayed had a 63 percent chance of winning, compared to a 65 percent chance on Polymarket. That marks a shift from earlier in August. On August 9, El-Sayed had only a 55 percent chance of winning on Kalshi as Democrats became increasingly concerned about his chances. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. A Contested Battleground Michigan has become an electoral battleground over the past decade. Former President Barack Obama easily won the state twice, by more than 16 points in 2008 and by just under 10 points in 2012. But Trump flipped it in 2016, carrying it by less than half a percentage point. Trump made gains across the state because of his strong showing among white voters in rural areas who backed Obama. He lost ground in the suburbs around Detroit and parts of Western Michigan around cities like Grand Rapids, but rural gains made up for it. Democrats struggled to win back those rural voters in significant numbers in recent cycles but continued to make gains in the suburbs. Michigan flipped back to Democrats in 2020, when Biden carried it by just under 2 points. But Trump won it again in 2024 by about 1.4 points—the strongest showing for a Republican presidential candidate since 1988. Michigan Is Must-Win State for Democrats The Michigan Senate has key national implications. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, so Democrats must defend all their seats and flip four others to take control of the upper chamber. Democrats are facing a difficult map, defending seats in two states Trump won in 2024—Georgia and Michigan. Polling in Georgia has been better for Democrats, showing Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff having a polling lead over Representative Mike Collins. Maine and North Carolina are viewed as Democrats’ top flip opportunities. In Maine, which Harris won by about 7 points, longtime GOP Senator Susan Collins is up for reelection. She faces Democrat Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president. Jackson took over the campaign after scandal-plagued Graham Platner exited the race following a primary victory. Collins has shown a remarkable ability to win elections in Maine as she seeks her sixth term. In North Carolina, which Trump won by about 3 points, former Governor Roy Cooper, a Democrat, has built a polling lead against Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee. Republican Senator Thom Tillis is retiring. But even if Democrats win all of those races, Republicans would still have a 51-49 majority, so Democrats must win at least two seats in double-digit Trump 2024 states to win a majority. Democrats view Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas as being potentially competitive, and polls show close races in those states. If Republicans flip Michigan, Democrats would then need to flip three of those seats, a more difficult feat given their conservative leans. Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.

news.title: As The City Prepares for Another Weekend Without Power, Gary Mayor Says Residents Deserve Better
news.text:
More than a week after a powerful storm tore through Northwest Indiana, thousands of Gary residents remain without electricity. Northern Indiana Public Service Company (NIPSCO) announced that power will be fully restored across Gary by Tuesday (Aug. 25). But for residents who could spend nearly two weeks without power, trying to survive the aftermath of the devastating storm feels like a crisis that refuses to end.

Gary Mayor Eddie Melton says his constituents deserve better information.

“Every single day, we’ve been providing an update on what’s going on post the storm since Aug. 11,” Melton said in an Instagram update. “The main thing I’m doing right now is demanding that NIPSCO give specific and accurate information regarding this outage,” he said, arguing that earlier restoration information was inadequate for Gary.

RELATED: VP Kamala Harris Gets Real About Environmental Racism

City workers, police, volunteers and General Services crews have been working around the clock to clear roads, remove trees and connect residents with food, clothing, shelter and information, according to the mayor’s office. Still, Gary residents are expressing their frustrations with what seems like communication errors and a lack of urgency from NIPSCO.

A city where Black residents represent over 75 percent of the population, Gary has faced severe environmental injustice for generations due to its heavy industrial concentration. Residents often experience disproportionate exposure to toxic air and higher health risks, according to the Pulitzer Center. This is coupled with historical housing discrimination and systemic disinvestment.

The latest blackout feels like another chapter in Gary’s complicated history of Black excellence and environmental neglect, a history that other Black cities, like New Orleans, have also faced.

Reporter Samantha Chatman asked Mayor Melton whether the crisis reminded him of Hurricane Katrina. 

“Well, it certainly feels that way at night,” the mayor responded, describing children walking in the dark trying to find food, stressing that Gary’s most vulnerable are being hit hardest.

“When you see senior citizens that’s calling, asking for assistance, it definitely feels that way,” he added. 

Hurricane Katrina devastated the Gulf Coast, killing hundreds and displacing thousands of people. To date, seven people in Gary have been confirmed dead due to the storm and blackout, according to officials. But it’s hard not to make comparisons. The slow response to Black residents of New Orleans impacted by Hurricane Katrina was widely criticized. Today, while NIPSCO works to restore the power, Gary is trying to take care of itself.

Melton said the city has been working with the YWCA and community partners to offer support to residents. City officials and volunteers have also been helping residents navigate the aftermath, including flooding, damaged homes, fallen trees and other storm-related problems.

The mayor urged residents dealing with damage and loss to document everything for future reimbursement. During an appearance on “The Breakfast Club,” he advised taking photos and videos of damaged property, saving receipts for emergency purchases, and keeping track of the dates and length of the outage. Residents should also contact their homeowners or renters insurance providers to ask if spoiled food, temporary lodging or other losses are covered under their policies. 

While the city prepares for another weekend in the dark, residents continue to show up for each other, and the mayor’s office continues to offer clear communication to keep everyone on the same page. For Melton, this is a reflection of the work the city has completed thus far and what remains to be done.

“Crime has been at the lowest it’s ever been in 60 years,” he said. “So that progress is not going to stop. It’s just slowed us down right now until we can get back to normal.”
news.summary:
After more than a week without power, Gary residents face mounting losses as Mayor Eddie Melton demands answers and pushes for recovery.

news.title: Amid anger at Trump, a moderate Republican in the suburbs tries to hold on
news.text:
Longtime state Sen. Jim Abeler won his last election by just 186 votes.Angie Nelson took notice.“He has been in office since I was in high school over 25 years ago,” said Nelson, his DFL challenger in this fall’s election. “He does not reflect who our community is now.”

Nelson said this to me on the capacious deck of Mike Gamache’s Andover home. Gamache is an Anoka County commissioner who hosted a volunteer night Monday for Nelson.

Indeed, Abeler has been in the Minnesota Legislature since 1998, when Randy Moss was starring as a Vikings rookie. He went from the House to the Senate in 2017. 

Related: Red state? Blue state? Here are the races that will likely determine party control at the Minnesota Legislature

And he did win reelection by just a hair in 2022, after (he is quick to tell you) the state Supreme Court redrew District 35 to make it bluer.

At the state Capitol, Abeler looms large. He cuts deals with Sen. John Hoffman, DFL-Champlin, on financing the state’s sprawling Medicaid program. He occasionally is the lone Republican to break from his party’s caucus.

But in his district, which comprises Anoka, Coon Rapids and a slice of Andover, Abeler is vulnerable. 

Voters here went for Kamala Harris and Tim Walz in the 2024 presidential election. The two state House representatives are DFLers Kari Rehrauer and Zack Stephenson. Plus, Hoffman is door-knocking for Nelson. 

Abeler is doing what he can to hang on. 

MinnPost has identified seven state Senate races that are basically toss-ups and critical to which party will control a chamber that now has 34 DFLers and 33 Republicans. In those nail-biters, Abeler is the only Republican to have more cash on hand than his opponent, as of last month. 

Plus, Abeler is door knocking “40 hours a week” during an uncomfortably hot summer. 

“The first Monday that was like a month-and-a-half ago, that was like, ‘Don’t go outside.’ I did 310 doors that day,” he told me as I followed him door-knocking one scalding August afternoon.

But Nelson, who is an elementary school principal, is also at doorsteps, and can paint a bleak picture about what she hears.

“Our community is in an urgent crisis,” she said.

A different kind of Republican

“We really are lacking collaborative leadership,” Abeler tells me, pushing his bike alongside an intricate loop of homeowner association condos with beige vinyl siding in Coon Rapids. “If I have a strength, that’s it.”

I followed Abeler door-to-door the afternoon after Republican primary voters selected Lisa Demuth as their pick for governor. Abeler preferred Demuth to the Donald Trump-endorsed Mike Lindell, but said that he could also work well with Amy Klobuchar. 

“We’re going to have a real election now,” he said of Demuth defeating Lindell. “She’s credible. Klobuchar’s credible.”

Abeler added that he can work productively with both the House speaker and the U.S. senator.

From 2022: Abeler-Rehrauer contest northwest of Twin Cities among 10 legislative races to watch in suburbs

But he is a Republican, as one person who answered the door pointed out. 

“Actually, I’m the kind of Republican that a lot of Democrats like. Green, labor-friendly, collaborates with everybody,” Abeler replied, citing endorsements from the SEIU, Minnesota Nurses Association and Conservation Minnesota Voter Center among other groups. 

“Trump’s kind of ruined it for some of us,” the woman at the door with a butterfly tattoo on her ankle said in response. “When I see a Republican, I see Trump. I mean, he’s ruined it. I don’t even like the American flag anymore.”

She then asked Abeler why he didn’t speak out about Operation Metro Surge.

Abeler responded that he wrote President Trump a letter in December criticizing his denigration of Somali immigrants, and that he tried to visit the Whipple Federal Building, where some people that federal immigration agents detained are held, but was turned away. 

Like the person at the door, Nelson has pushed Abeler to articulate his stance on a federal immigration enforcement strategy that left two Minneapolis demonstrators dead and over 3,500 Minnesotans detained. 

Nelson criticized Abeler for voting against a bill to rein in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) through actions like a ban on agents wearing masks and letting people sue agents. 

Abeler said he voted against the bill because it became a sprawling catchall. He was the lone Senate Republican to support a measure providing economic assistance to businesses affected by Operation Metro Surge, legislation that the House torpedoed.

Nelson characterized Abeler as a skillful chameleon who still votes much more with Republicans than not, all while retaining his folksy, riffing demeanor. 

“I really think he’s a nice person,” Nelson said. “Super nice person. But nice isn’t getting the work done.”

What Nelson cares about

Nelson led with housing and infrastructure in our interview. 

“I’ve seen my community that I live in deteriorate over time,” she said. “At least for Coon Rapids, it’s kind of turned into a place that people drive through instead of go to.”

Nelson wants more lanes in the stretch of U.S. Highway 10 that cuts across the district, complaining of constant bottlenecks. She also wants the state to pitch in with more funding for state Highways 65 and 252. 

As for housing, Nelson believes it would be appropriate for the state government to step in with zoning parameters. “We have a lot of empty buildings and empty lots that could potentially be rezoned for housing where we could bring in new families,” she said. 

Abeler believes zoning is an inherently local government function and does not want the state involved. I asked Nelson how her idea could overcome potential NIMBYism. 

“I think it depends on how you are approaching it,” she responded. “Nobody likes to see the abandoned buildings. They’re eyesores. They need to be managed sooner than later.”

While Abeler has a part-time chiropractic practice, Nelson is a full-time elementary school principal and former high school principal, on top of being a single mother of two teenagers. She said she is not taking a leave of absence for the campaign, but, if elected, would take leave during the legislative session. 

Being a principal is a lot like being a state senator, Nelson said, in that she must listen to a variety of different concerns. “It doesn’t mean that every person who comes to me, I’m going to agree, or just give them what they want,” she said. “But I will hear you.”

Abeler has gained a reputation as a dealmaker on Medicaid, the health insurance program for the poor, elderly and disabled that, including federal funding, makes up one-third of the state’s budget. 

Nelson said she would vie to join education committees, which also handle about one-third of state spending. 

A contrast in styles

Like Abeler, Nelson is an enthusiastic proponent of door knocking.

“We have 78 days until the election,” she said, addressing several volunteers seated around Gamache’s dining room table. “We have knocked over 17,000 doors. I have some of you to thank for that.”

“I got an electric scooter,” she added later, her counterpart to Abeler’s bike. “And it is life-changing. I am only five foot three and a half and I can only go so fast.”

But the candidates appear different in temperament. 

During a debate Wednesday night at Coon Rapids City Hall, Nelson was more formal and immediate.

“People are suffering and cannot afford their life right now,” she said, pinning part of the blame on Republican-initiated cuts of Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, otherwise known as food stamps, at the federal level.

Abeler was casual, full of asides like, “Well, it is more of a thought than a rebuttal,” and “Two minutes is not enough time to answer that question.”

He did not share Nelson’s vision that the district is in peril, stating, “Anoka, Coon Rapids and Andover are cities that actually work.”

At times, Abeler played up his experience. 

When Nelson mentioned, “We need more apprenticeships and fellowships” at Anoka-Ramsey Community College, Abeler said he was part of a group of legislators that helped keep the college running. 

Abeler also raised questions about the role of state senator itself and whether Nelson, or any rank-and-file legislator, had the power to act on their priorities. 

“Do you think it’s one person that gets to do something?” he rhetorically asked Nelson in a mostly empty Coon Rapids council chambers. “The major conference committees meet privately, and then they just announce it. It’s ugly.”

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to reflect that it was the state Supreme Court, not the legislature, that redrew District 35 in 2020.
news.summary:
State Sen. Jim Abeler has been in the Minnesota Legislature since the 1990s. But he faces a strong DFL challenger.

news.title: Ariana Grande calls out Donald Trump after her music appears in anti-trans TikTok
news.text: Ariana Grande has delivered a sharp rebuke to Donald Trump after his team featured her music in an anti-trans TikTok video . A clip uploaded to TikTok by Team Trump on Thursday showed the president striding towards the stage at a political rally. Text overlaying the footage declared: "Me and my truth we sit in silence... men can't have babies and should never compete in women's sports." Team Trump accompanied the post with the caption: "This decision shouldn't be controversial! #trump #arianagrande #maga." The video originally included Grande's 2024 hit We Can't Be Friends (Wait for Your Love), though the audio has now been removed. Grande hit back in the comments, marking yet another instance where she's been forced to challenge Trump's unauthorised use of her work. In her August 20 response, Grande wrote: "Never use my music again. Also, your truth is false", reports the Mirror US . This is the second time Grande has confronted Trump over music usage. Previously in June, the 33 year old pop sensation warned Trump against incorporating her song in an anti-ICE TikTok. That row began when the White House used her 2024 track Bye in a TikTok video showing ICE agents making arrests. The clip depicted ICE officers handcuffing several individuals. The clip was captioned: "Bye-bye. President Trump has delivered the most secure border in history." Grande responded sharply, writing: "Please do not ever use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense. F- ICE." Both her comment and the track have since been deleted from the TikTok post. While Grande's remark disappeared from the TikTok footage, a spokesperson for the pop star verified to Billboard that it was authentically Grande who left the comment and noted it had vanished "for some reason." Grande also took aim at the Trump administration during the 2026 Golden Globe Awards ceremony, where the Wicked star sported an ICE Out pin. In September 2025, Grande reshared an Instagram message condemning Trump regarding ICE operations and anti-trans language. The initial post was penned by activist Matt Bernstein and stated: "I want to check in with trump voters. I have one very genuine question. It's been 250 days. now that immigrants have been violently torn from their families and communities have been destroyed. "Now that trans people have been blamed for virtually everything and live in fear, now that free speech is on the brink of collapse for us all - has your life gotten better?" Throughout the 2024 presidential race, Grande backed Democratic contender Kamala Harris. She had previously taken to the stage for Barack Obama and Michelle Obama at the 2014 In Performance at the White House: Women of Soul occasion.
news.summary: Ariana Grande has issued a warning to Donald Trump after his team used her music in an anti-trans TikTok video, with the singer telling the president to "never use my music again"

news.title: On Michael Cohen’s Radio Show, Donald Trump Is Back to Being the “Boss”
news.text:
“The American people have spoken and re-elected Donald Trump,” Cohen wrote in an email. “Accordingly, I believe we must all acknowledge and respect the office of the Presidency and dismiss the case forthwith.”
Shocking as this development was, in retrospect, it may have been a preview of the reconciliation to come. Ever since Trump was reelected and guaranteed a return to the kind of power to which Cohen, by his own account in his memoirs and courtroom testimony, has long been drawn, the two men who had previously described one another as “fraud” and “rat” have been inching towards a full-fledged reunion: first, Cohen said earlier this year that he had “felt compelled and coerced to deliver what [prosecutors] were seeking.” Then he met with Trump at Mar-a-Lago and his Bedminster golf club. Cohen had orchestrated the payment to Stormy Daniels that in part sent him to prison in 2019, testifying in 2024 that he had done so at Trump’s direction. But on Thursday night, a month into his new role as a host on the Trump-aligned billionaire John Catsimatidis’s New York radio station, his tenor was ecstatic as he introduced his biggest guest to date.
“Tonight,” Cohen said, “you are tuning into something that people thought that they would never live to see.”
“Hello, Michael,” Trump said as he called in.
Such was Cohen’s early admiration for Trump that he bought two apartments at Trump World Tower in the 2000s. They first connected after Trump appreciated Cohen’s ferocious approach in a dispute with the building’s condo board, and the Long Island-bred lawyer has evinced a flair for melodrama at every turn in their roller-coaster relationship since, releasing books titled Disloyal and Revenge after emerging from prison in 2020. He was in rare form this week as he geared up for the interview with his old boss, explaining to listeners that “forgiveness does not mean amnesia” or “that the pain was fake or that I have forgotten a single second of what transpired.”
“Can loyalty survive the ultimate fallout?” Cohen went on, seeming to stretch the limits of his poetic capacities. “Can friendship exist after deep betrayal? Can two people who stood together at the summit and then tore each other apart in the valley actually find common ground again?”
To be sure, Cohen may have an ulterior motive for this dizzying rapprochement. He told CNN on Thursday that he had submitted a pardon application to the White House and planned to follow up the next day; Trump is currently appealing his felony conviction related to the infamous hush-money payment. “I respect the fact that you recanted everything you said,” Trump told Cohen on the air. “And that’s a big thing that you did.” (While it’s not clear what Cohen has privately said to Trump, he has not retracted the testimony he gave under oath.)
With that out of the way, Trump began to ramble: about Iran, about Venezuela, about how “the rallies are potentially bigger than ever,” about how Kamala Harris “knew less about the border than a child would know.” Cohen barely got a word in, but he slipped into reminiscence easily: “Boss, you remember when I was by your side?” During the decade-long period when Cohen played Trump’s antagonist in a national psychodrama, he looked agitated and haggard, but now, he sounded as if he had stepped back into a prior state of exhilarated comfort that had never quite worn off. In Disloyal, Cohen asks himself about the source of his “starstruck, moth-to-the-flame compulsion to insinuate [himself] with a man so transparently problematic in myriad ways.”
The answer, he wrote, “included something deeper than the obvious lures of money and power, though those were crucial factors. It was physical, emotional, not quite spiritual, but a deep longing and need that Trump filled for me. Around Trump I felt excited, alive, like he possessed the urgent and only truth, the chance for my salvation and success in life.”
news.summary: After a long, vicious feud that ricocheted across the national press and a Manhattan courtroom, the president and his former fixer reunited this week on Cohen’s radio show for an interview that immediately slipped into a cozy rapport of kindred spirits.
